headline: Gold leaps 3.6% to $4,680 as safe-haven demand surges, PLS rockets nearly 5% on ASX, and the Warriors storm to the top of the NRL ladder.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS had a strong session today, jumping nearly 5% to $5.07. No single headline drove it, but lithium stocks have been catching a bid broadly — likely a combination of short covering and some renewed optimism about the lithium price outlook. It's still well below your cost base though, so this is a bounce rather than a turnaround — keep watching.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS slipped 1.3% today to $528. This ASX-listed ETF tracks the entire US share market, so it tends to move with overnight US sentiment — last night's Wall St session was actually up slightly, so today's dip is likely currency-related (the stronger Aussie dollar reduces the AUD value of US-denominated holdings). Nothing structural to worry about here.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI eased back about 1% today to $16.20. There was no specific news — the AI ETF sector had a quiet session. This holding is still sitting at a 14% loss overall, which stings, but the long-term AI growth story remains very much intact. No reason to panic.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG dipped a modest 0.48% today to $76.91. As a diversified fund holding global and Australian shares, it tracks broad market movements. A small dip on a slightly soft ASX day — nothing to read into this at all.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE ticked up 0.24% today to $93.56 — a quiet, slightly positive session. Emerging markets were steady. Still fractionally below your cost base overall, but nothing notable happening here.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG gained 1.05% last night to $341.75 — its best daily move this week. The catalyst: continued momentum from growing AI user numbers and strong ad revenue, per market commentary. Android Pulse on Google Play also crossed 10 million installs, adding to positive sentiment around the Google ecosystem.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: MSFT edged up 0.43% last night to $483.24. Azure cloud growth holding at 40% is keeping analyst targets elevated — one forecast has MSFT potentially breaking $570. Steady, solid session with no specific negative catalysts.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO was essentially flat last night, dipping just 0.22% to $239.62. Big GTA VI pre-order numbers are a genuine positive for the long-term story, though Rockstar issuing legal subpoenas to Microsoft and Discord over GTA 6 leaks is a minor distraction. The underlying investment case — GTA VI launch — is very much on track.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX surging — bounce or breakout?
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals jumped nearly 5% today to $5.07, one of the strongest movers on the ASX. You're still sitting at a 24.8% overall loss on this one, so today's move is welcome but doesn't fix the hole yet. For a long-term holder, the question is whether the lithium price cycle is turning — this is worth watching over coming weeks. No need to act today, but keep an eye on whether this momentum holds.

watch_today.title: Gold smashing records — your VDHG and VTS have exposure
watch_today.detail: Gold spiked 3.6% last night to $4,680/oz — a massive single-day move. This suggests real safe-haven demand, probably linked to geopolitical tension (Israel-Turkey risk, Iran warnings to neighbours). Gold at these levels is a tailwind for any fund with resource/commodity exposure. VDHG holds some diversified commodity exposure and VTS holds US-listed gold miners indirectly. No action needed, but the signal is worth noting.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — still underwater, long-term thesis intact
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF is down 14.2% overall and slipped another 1% today. No specific bad news — just a quiet session. The AI investment story hasn't changed; the sector is still growing fast. For a buy-and-hold investor, sitting on a paper loss in a growth theme like this is normal. Nothing to do here except stay patient.

watch_today.title: TTWO — GTA VI pre-orders eye-watering, Rockstar chasing leakers
watch_today.detail: Take-Two/Rockstar Games is issuing legal subpoenas to Microsoft and Discord over GTA 6 leaks, showing the company is aggressively protecting its biggest release. Pre-order numbers are being described as 'eye-watering' by Mashable. TTWO was essentially flat last night (-0.22%). The long-term case for this stock is the GTA VI launch — that story is intact and building steam. Hold confidently.

watch_today.title: Iran warns neighbours: joining US economic war means becoming an 'enemy'
watch_today.detail: Iran's new security chief has drawn a sharp line in the sand — any neighbouring country that participates in US-led economic pressure on Iran will be treated as an enemy state. This ratchets up Middle East tension, which is partly why oil and gold are both elevated. Worth monitoring if you have any emerging markets exposure (VGE holds some Middle East-adjacent countries).

watch_today.title: GOOG & MSFT — both gaining, AI tailwind continuing
watch_today.detail: Both your big US tech holdings moved up last night — GOOG +1.05% and MSFT +0.43%. Alphabet is seeing AI user growth and ad revenue expansion; Microsoft's Azure cloud is holding 40% growth. Both are in good shape for long-term holders. No action needed — just a reassuring data point.

world.summary: A tense weekend globally — Iran draws a hard line on its neighbours, a potential Israel-Turkey war raises NATO questions, Lebanon's economy is in freefall, and the Pentagon is purging independent voices from military media.

stories.title: Iran's new security chief warns neighbours: side with the US and you're our enemy
stories.why_it_matters: Iran's newly appointed security chief has issued a stark warning: any neighbouring country that joins the US-led economic pressure campaign against Iran will be officially considered an enemy of the state. This is a significant escalation in Iran's regional posture — it essentially threatens countries like Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Iraq with retribution if they align with Washington's sanctions. For everyday Australians, this matters because Middle East instability affects global oil prices and can ripple through to petrol costs and inflation. It's also a warning sign for emerging market investors with exposure to the region.

stories.title: Could an Israel-Turkey war trigger NATO's Article 5?
stories.why_it_matters: Analysts are now seriously asking whether an armed conflict between Israel and Turkey — both involved in the broader Middle East tensions — could activate NATO's Article 5, the 'an attack on one is an attack on all' clause. Turkey is a NATO member, which creates a deeply complicated legal and military scenario. If Article 5 were triggered, it could theoretically drag Western nations (including Australia's allies) into a conflict. This is still a hypothetical, but the fact it's being debated seriously tells you how elevated regional tensions have become.

stories.title: World Bank: Lebanon's economy to shrink 6.4% because of war
stories.why_it_matters: The World Bank is projecting Lebanon's economy will contract by 6.4% this year due to ongoing war. This is on top of years of economic collapse that has already wiped out the savings of millions of Lebanese. A 6.4% contraction is severe — it means businesses closing, unemployment rising, and basic services deteriorating further. Lebanon's crisis also puts pressure on neighbouring countries dealing with refugee flows and regional instability.

stories.title: Pentagon fires editor and publisher of independent military publication
stories.why_it_matters: The Pentagon has sacked the editor and publisher of an independent military publication — a move that's raising serious press freedom concerns in the US. Independent military journalism plays a critical watchdog role, reporting on defence policy, troop welfare, and accountability issues that official channels often don't cover. Firing editorial staff at a publication that scrutinises the military sends a chilling message to other outlets and journalists covering US defence matters.

stories.title: Ed Martin leaves DOJ to focus on 'legal battles' in upcoming US elections
stories.why_it_matters: Trump has announced that Ed Martin is leaving his role at the Department of Justice to focus on 'legal battles' related to upcoming elections. Martin was a controversial appointment — a Trump loyalist placed inside the DOJ. His departure to work on election-related legal strategy suggests the administration is already gearing up for potential disputes over election results or voting processes. This is worth watching as the US moves closer to its next election cycle.

markets.summary: The ASX closed slightly lower today (-0.27%) while last night's Wall St session was quietly positive — S&P 500 and NASDAQ both up 0.43%. The big story is gold, which surged 3.6% to $4,680/oz on safe-haven demand. The Aussie dollar strengthened to 71.75 US cents, which mutes some of the gains on your US holdings when converted back to AUD.

indicators.note: Soft close today, down 0.27% — nothing dramatic, just a mildly cautious session.

indicators.name: S&P 500

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite

politics.summary: Quiet weekend in Australian politics, with debate continuing around inflation, the digital news bargaining framework, and some currency wobble from softer jobs data earlier in the week.

stories.title: Fixing Australia's inflation problem
stories.why_it_matters: The ongoing debate about how to get Australian inflation back under control is continuing in policy circles. Australia's inflation has proven stubborn compared to other developed countries, which is why the RBA (Reserve Bank) has been slow to cut interest rates. For everyday Australians, sticky inflation means mortgage repayments stay higher for longer and cost-of-living pressure doesn't ease quickly. This is an opinion piece rather than breaking news, but it reflects a live policy tension heading into the next RBA meeting.

stories.title: Weak jobs data revives bets on RBA rate cuts
stories.why_it_matters: Earlier this week, softer-than-expected Australian jobs data prompted traders to increase their bets that the RBA will cut interest rates. The Aussie dollar slipped on that news (though it has since recovered). A rate cut — where the RBA lowers the official interest rate — would be good news for mortgage holders (cheaper repayments) and for growth assets like shares. Markets are now pricing in a higher chance of a cut in the next few months. If this plays out, it's a tailwind for the ASX.

stories.title: News media bargaining levy changes to give smaller publishers a bigger share
stories.why_it_matters: The federal government is finalising changes to Australia's news media bargaining framework — the system that requires big tech platforms (like Google and Meta) to pay Australian news publishers for using their content. Final changes aim to ensure smaller, regional publishers get a fairer slice of the money, not just the big mastheads. This is relevant for Alphabet (GOOG) investors to note — it's an ongoing cost and compliance burden for Google in Australia, though not material enough to move the stock.

ai.summary: A thin week for AI news — the main story is a debate in the US about whether AI is actually being regulated at all, with critics arguing the regulatory vacuum is a real problem.

stories.title: 'Hardly any' AI regulations — critics say the US is dangerously under-prepared
stories.why_it_matters: Former US Health Secretary Xavier Becerra is drawing attention to the glaring lack of AI regulation in the United States, calling out claims that there are 'hardly any' rules governing how AI can be used in high-stakes areas like healthcare, employment, and law enforcement. While individual US states have passed some AI rules, there's no comprehensive federal law — meaning companies can largely do what they want with AI systems. For investors in AI-heavy stocks like GOOG and MSFT, this regulatory gap is a double-edged sword: short-term, it means fewer compliance costs and faster deployment, but longer-term it creates the risk of sudden heavy-handed regulation if something goes badly wrong.

stories.title: Microsoft Azure growth holds at 40% — analysts eye $570 price target for MSFT
stories.why_it_matters: Microsoft's Azure cloud platform — essentially the infrastructure that powers AI services, apps, and businesses globally — is maintaining 40% year-on-year growth, which is exceptional for a business of its size. Analysts at TradingKey are now suggesting MSFT could break $570, implying roughly 18% upside from current levels. This growth is being driven almost entirely by AI workloads — companies paying Microsoft to run AI tools and store data. For MSFT holders, this is a strong signal that the AI revenue story is real and not just hype.

stories.title: Alphabet stock rises as AI users and ad revenue grow
stories.why_it_matters: Alphabet (Google's parent company) is seeing a virtuous cycle: more people using Google's AI tools means more engagement, which means more ad impressions, which means more revenue. This is the core of why GOOG stock has been rising — AI isn't just a cost for Google, it's driving real revenue growth. Android Pulse on Google Play separately crossed 10 million installs, showing Google's ecosystem products are also gaining traction. The market is increasingly rewarding Alphabet for demonstrating that AI investment translates into actual profit.

sport.summary: Big NRL weekend: the Warriors are sitting on top of the NRL ladder after thrashing the Rabbitohs 45-26, the Bulldogs demolished the Dragons 44-14, and the Sea Eagles belted the Knights 44-24. In AFL, the Crows and Cats both locked in top-six spots. The Roosters vs Tigers game was still live at the time of this digest.

stories.title: Warriors storm to top of NRL ladder with 45-26 demolition of Rabbitohs
stories.why_it_matters: The Warriors put on a masterclass in Round 25, running up their highest score of the season in a 45-26 belting of South Sydney at Accor Stadium. The win puts the Warriors top of the NRL ladder — albeit by the narrowest margin possible on for-and-against. It's a remarkable rise for a team that has historically struggled to stay in finals contention. They'll need to hold their form over the final rounds to lock in a top-four spot.

stories.title: Bulldogs crush Dragons 44-14; Sea Eagles belt Knights 44-24
stories.why_it_matters: Two big scorelines from Saturday's NRL action. Canterbury Bulldogs put 44 points on the Dragons (14) at Allianz Stadium, continuing their strong form and putting pressure on the teams above them in the eight. Manly Sea Eagles were equally ruthless, hammering Newcastle Knights 44-24 at McDonald Jones — a result that does Newcastle's finals hopes no favours at all. Manly look ominous heading into the finals series.

stories.title: Sharks beat Titans 30-22 in Round 25 Sunday clash
stories.why_it_matters: The Cronulla Sharks came from behind to beat the Gold Coast Titans 30-22 at Cbus Super Stadium today — a result that stings for local Gold Coast fans. Titans were competitive but couldn't hold on in the second half. The Sharks continue to push for a top-four finish with the win.

stories.title: AFL: Crows and Cats both lock in top-six spots with big wins
stories.why_it_matters: In AFL, Adelaide Crows secured their top-six spot with a commanding win over GWS Giants, while Geelong Cats also locked in a top-six finish with a dominant performance this weekend. Both results mean these clubs have guaranteed finals footy — a huge deal heading into the business end of the AFL season. Meanwhile, Collingwood and Carlton's finals dreams have apparently taken a hit — the AFL world was stunned by results that closed the door for both clubs.
